justice: The corridor allocates substantial space to motor traffic with multiple wide vehicle lanes, while pedestrian space is pushed to the road edge, indicating an uneven spatial balance among users.

A bus stop is visible on the left side and another stop/sign structure appears on the right, showing that public transport users are at least partly served rather than the street functioning only for private cars.

Side sidewalks appear present and buffered by hedges and trees, but no visible marked crosswalk, curb ramp detail, or tactile paving can be confirmed in the image, limiting clearly inclusive access for all users.
safety: The roadway has clear lane arrows, lane markings, a central median, and roadside guardrails, which help organize movements and reduce random conflicts between directions of travel.
Tall streetlights line the corridor, suggesting better night visibility and traffic safety conditions than an unlit arterial.
Safety is reduced for non-motorized users because the road is very wide, vehicle speeds are likely high, and no visible pedestrian crossing or protected bicycle facility is seen in the frame.
livability: Continuous rows of trees and hedges on both sides improve environmental quality and make the arterial feel less harsh than a fully paved corridor.
The visible bus stop infrastructure supports basic mobility and can connect people to daily destinations, contributing modestly to everyday usability.

Livability remains limited because the street edge shows little active frontage, no visible shops or social spaces, and the overall environment is dominated by fast-moving traffic rather than human-scale activity.
sustainability: The presence of bus stop facilities indicates support for shared and lower-carbon travel modes beyond private automobiles.
Extensive roadside trees, hedges, and median planting provide urban greenery that can contribute to cooling, air-quality benefits, and ecological value.
Sustainability is constrained by the very large paved carriageway devoted to multiple motor lanes, which signals a transport landscape still heavily oriented toward car use.
aesthetics: The avenue has a clean, orderly appearance with consistent streetlights, trimmed hedges, and well-maintained pavement, creating strong visual coherence.
Tree-lined edges and green medians soften the scale of the broad road and add visual relief to what would otherwise be a highly engineered setting.
Aesthetic quality is somewhat reduced by the oversized asphalt surface and sparse building presence, which make the scene feel infrastructural rather than richly place-based.
comfort: Rows of roadside trees provide some shade and thermal buffering along the edges, which is better than an entirely exposed roadway.
The pavement appears smooth and well maintained for drivers and likely also benefits bus travel quality, supporting physical comfort for motorized users.
Comfort for pedestrians and cyclists is weaker because the corridor is extremely wide, visually dominated by traffic lanes, and likely exposed to traffic noise and heat away from the tree line.
walkability: Sidewalk space appears to exist along the right side and possibly the left side, so walking is accommodated at least at the margin of the corridor.
Walkability is limited by the long crossing distance created by the many traffic lanes and the absence of any clearly visible zebra crossing or pedestrian refuge crossing point in the image.
The street lacks strong pedestrian-oriented features such as benches, active frontages, curb-extension crossings, or visible wayfinding, making it functional but not inviting for walking.
bikeability: No clearly marked or protected bicycle lane is visible on the main carriageway, which substantially lowers perceived and actual cycling safety.
The width and likely speed of motor traffic create a stressful riding environment for most cyclists, especially where turning lanes and multiple through lanes are present.

Although side greenery and a relatively orderly road layout help legibility, there is no visible bicycle parking, bike markings, or separation elements that would make cycling convenient or comfortable.
